newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thailand expects better times after baht float.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thailand expects better times after baht float.

text.p: Thai officials on Friday painted a rosy future for the economy after the baht's shock devaluation, with the troubled finance sector stabilising, exports improving and the current account deficit narrowing.
But they warned growth could continue to slow and said inflation could be whipped up in the wake of the de facto devaluation.
"I hope the worst is over," Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee told a briefing of foreign journalists.
"Never mind the economic growth. From day one that this government took office, our first priority was to restore financial stability," he said.
"Economic recovery was the second priority. Without stability, the economy cannot recover."
Thailand is gripped by its worst economic slump in over a decade and 1997 economic growth is set to slow to 5.6 percent from 6.4 percent in 1996, according to official estimates.
Private economists tip a far gloomier scenario with growth scaled back to between three and five percent.
Narongchai said with all the measures prescribed by the finance authorities, the ailing finance sector should recover towards the end of the year.

The government has sought to bolster the cash-strapped finance sector by issuing urgent decrees encouraging more mergers and acquisitions and allowing greater foreign equity in financial institutions.

It also attempted to contain the crisis by suspending the operation of 16 financially distressed finance firms, forcing them to produce concrete future plans or lose their licences and be absorbed by healthy companies.
Wednesday's surprise announcement of a "managed float" of the baht, which translates into an effective devaluation, would bring much needed liquidity into Thailand's economy, Narongchai said.
"We will end up with much less but stronger financial institutions. For the rest of the year, we will see slow recovery of the sector," he said.

"If the exchange rate remained the same, no one will invest here. With the baht now being determined by market forces, investors can make their own risk assessment and be more confident to come in," he said.
Narongchai said he also saw a sign of recovery in exports, considered crucial to the economic turnaround at a time when Thailand must slow down investment to narrow the current account deficit.
He projected that the current account gap would shrink to below five percent of gross domestic product.
The export growth target for 1997, currently set by the ministry at 10 percent, would be revised after a meeting with exporters, he added.
Thailand's January-April exports grew 2.4 percent year-on-year. Thai exports had been sluggish recently and in 1996 growth contracted 0.2 percent from a boom of more than 23 percent in 1995.
